challenges.name: config-from-env-quiz
challenges.title: Where does the configuration come from?
challenges.description: Three statements about how Rice Rocket's api got its configuration in the two incidents of this lesson, and about a secret mounted by Compose. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: When a container sets an environment variable at run time, what happens to the value the image was built with: is it replaced inside the image, or only shadowed in that one container?
Look at how `parseInt` treats a string that starts with digits and continues with letters, and compare it with `Number`.
Postgres' official image takes `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db_password`: try working out why it needs a variable that holds a path rather than the password.

questions.question:
The incident review found this line in the api Dockerfile. Since then, the staging compose file sets its own `DATABASE_URL`:

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV DATABASE_URL=postgres://rice:Pr0d-pass@prod-db.internal:5432/rice_rocket
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

```yaml
# compose.staging.yml
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/rice-rocket/api:1.4.0
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://rice:stg-pass@staging-db:5432/rice_rocket
```

Statement: "Now that staging sets `DATABASE_URL` at run time, the production password can no longer be read by anyone who can pull the image."
questions.explanation: False. `ENV` is written into the image configuration. A run-time value only shadows it inside that one container; the image still carries the production URL, and `docker image inspect` (or `docker history`) prints it for anyone who can pull the image. The common misconception is that overriding a variable removes it. The fix is to delete the line, rebuild, and rotate the password, because every image already pushed keeps it.

questions.question:
The second incident. The api reads its port like this, and the container was started with a typo in the variable:

```javascript
const port = parseInt(process.env.PORT ?? "3000", 10);
server.listen(port, () => log.info(`listening on ${port}`));
```

```text
$ docker compose exec api printenv PORT
30OO
$ docker compose logs api
api-1  | {"level":"info","msg":"listening on 30"}
```

Statement: "`parseInt` stopped at the first character that is not a digit, so the api started on port 30 without reporting any error."
questions.explanation: True. `parseInt("30OO", 10)` reads the leading digits `30` and ignores the rest (the letters O); it only returns NaN when the string does not start with a digit. The api listened on 30 while Nginx and the healthcheck called 3000. The common misconception is that parseInt validates its input. Check the whole string, for example with `/^\d+$/` and a 1-65535 range, and refuse to start otherwise.

questions.question:
To keep the JWT signing key out of the image and out of `docker inspect`, the team moves it to a Compose secret:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: registry.example.com/rice-rocket/api:1.4.0
    secrets:
      - jwt_secret

secrets:
  jwt_secret:
    file: ./secrets/jwt_secret.txt
```

Statement: "Inside the api container, `process.env.JWT_SECRET` now holds the content of `jwt_secret.txt`."
questions.explanation: False. A Compose secret is mounted as a file, at `/run/secrets/jwt_secret` here; it does not create any environment variable. The api has to read the file, which is why the usual convention is a second variable that holds the path, such as `JWT_SECRET_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_secret`. The common misconception is that secrets are a protected kind of environment variable; keeping them as files is the point, since environment variables show up in `docker inspect` and are inherited by child processes.

challenges.name: load-config-from-env
challenges.title: Fail fast on a bad environment
challenges.description:
Assemble `loadConfig(env, files)` for the api: it runs once at startup and either returns the whole configuration or stops the container with every problem listed. `env` is an object like `process.env` (strings or undefined; a variable set to "" counts as not set). `files` maps a path to its content and stands in for the files mounted in the container, such as Docker secrets under /run/secrets/.

Rules: PORT is decimal digits only, from 1 to 65535, default 3000 (returned as a number). DATABASE_URL is required and must start with postgres:// or postgresql://. LOG_LEVEL is one of debug, info, warn, error, default info. The JWT secret comes from JWT_SECRET, or from the file whose path is in JWT_SECRET_FILE with its trailing line break (\n or \r\n) removed; setting both is an error, and an empty secret counts as missing.

Collect every problem, then throw ONE Error whose message is the problems sorted alphabetically (plain `sort()`) and joined with "; ". The exact problem texts: `PORT must be an integer from 1 to 65535, got "<value>"` · `DATABASE_URL is required` · `DATABASE_URL must start with postgres:// or postgresql://` (never echo the URL: it holds the password) · `LOG_LEVEL must be one of debug, info, warn, error, got "<value>"` · `JWT_SECRET or JWT_SECRET_FILE is required` · `JWT_SECRET and JWT_SECRET_FILE are both set` · `JWT_SECRET_FILE not found: <path>`.

Without problems, return a frozen object `{ port, databaseUrl, logLevel, jwtSecret }`. Run shows `{ ok: true, frozen, config }` or `{ ok: false, errors }`, where errors is your message split on "; ". The editor holds the finished function with its blocks missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line: fill every line with a piece. Some pieces are wrong on purpose, so check each one against the rules above.
hints: If PORT is "30OO", what does each of `parseInt`, `Number` and a digits-only regular expression give you, and which one lets you say no?

Look at where your function throws: an early `throw` reports one problem per deploy. Push each problem into an array and throw once at the end; for the secret file, look at the last characters of the file content.

The same shape on other input: a `RETRY_LIMIT` that must be 0-10 with default 3 reads the raw string, checks it against `/^\d+$/` and the range, pushes `RETRY_LIMIT must be ..., got "<value>"` on failure, and only uses the number once the text is valid.
